title: Data Interpretation
intro: Reading data from tables and graphs is one of the most common SAT Problem-Solving and Data Analysis skills. This chapter covers tables, bar graphs, pie charts, histograms, line graphs and scatterplots. Read each topic, work the problems with the hint ladder, then take the 8-question topic test.

items.name: Total
items.formula: add every value in the set

items.name: Average
items.formula: sum of values ÷ number of values

topics.name: Tables
topics.details: A table organises data in rows and columns. SAT questions ask you to read individual values, then combine them — usually a total, a difference, an average, or which category is greatest or least. The skill is locating the exact cell the question refers to and not confusing a row label with its value. Add carefully when a question asks for a total, and subtract the correct pair for a difference. A common trap is answering with one of the raw values when the question actually wants a computed result, so reread what is being asked before choosing.

solved.problem: A table lists units sold: Mon 12, Tue 18, Wed 9, Thu 21. What is the total?
Using the same data, how many more were sold on Thursday than Wednesday?
A table shows scores 80, 76, 90, 74. What is the mean?
A table shows sales A 40, B 55, C 35, D 50. Which is greatest?
solved.solution: The largest value is 55, which is B.

unsolved.problem: A table shows visitors: Fri 30, Sat 45, Sun 25. What is the total?
Tickets sold: matinee 60, evening 95. How many more in the evening?
hints: Subtract the smaller from the larger.

unsolved.problem: A table shows 4 test scores: 70, 85, 90, 75. What is the average?
Books read: A 12, B 9, C 15, D 11. Which student read the fewest?
A table shows rainfall (mm): Jan 40, Feb 30, Mar 50. What is the total for the quarter?

topics.name: Bar Graphs
topics.details: A bar graph shows quantities as bars whose heights represent values, making comparisons easy to see at a glance. Read each bar against the scale on the axis — the most common error is misreading the scale when gridlines jump by 2, 5 or 10 rather than 1. Questions ask for totals, differences between bars, the tallest or shortest bar, or how a value would change. Treat a bar graph exactly like a table once you have read off the heights: add for a total, subtract a pair for a difference, and compare heights to find the greatest or least.

solved.problem: A bar graph shows goals: A 3, B 5, C 2, D 6. What is the total?
Using the same graph, how many more goals did D score than A?
Bars show 10, 14, 9, 21 cars washed. Which day had the most?
If a bar of height 8 doubled, what would its new height be?

unsolved.problem: A bar graph shows trees planted: A 7, B 12, C 5. What is the total?
Bars show 18 and 11 packages. How many more is the taller bar?
Bars: Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15. Which is tallest?
A bar of height 9 triples. What is the new height?
Bars: A 6, B 6, C 9, D 4. What is the total?

topics.name: Pie Charts
topics.details: A pie chart shows how a whole is divided into parts, each slice a percentage of the total. The percentages always add to 100. To find how many items a slice represents, multiply its percentage (as a decimal) by the total: a 40% slice of 600 is 0.40 × 600 = 240. To find a slice’s central angle, multiply its percentage by 360°, since the whole circle is 360°. The frequent mistake is treating the percentage itself as the count. Always check whether the question wants a count, a percentage, an angle, or a fraction of the whole.

solved.problem: A pie chart: Bus 40% of 600 students. How many take the bus?
A 25% slice — what is its central angle?
A pie chart shows Rent 30% of a $2,000 budget. How much is rent?
If three slices are 20%, 35% and 25%, what percent is the fourth?

unsolved.problem: A 20% slice of 500 books — how many books?
What central angle matches a 50% slice?
A pie chart: Food 25% of a $1,200 budget. How much on food?
Slices are 45%, 30% and the rest. What percent is the rest?
A 10% slice of 800 visitors — how many visitors?

topics.name: Histograms
topics.details: A histogram groups numerical data into intervals (bins) and shows how many values fall in each bin with bars. Unlike a bar graph of categories, the bars sit on a continuous number scale. Questions ask for the total count (add all the frequencies), how many fall above or below a cut-off (add the relevant bins), or which interval is most common (the tallest bar). When a cut-off such as “at least 60” is given, include every bin from that point up. Be careful with interval boundaries and read the frequency, not the interval label, as the value you add.

solved.problem: Using the same data, how many scored at least 60?
Which interval is most common?
solved.solution: The tallest bar is 12, the 40–60 interval.

solved.problem: How many scored below 40?

unsolved.problem: Bins 0–10:4, 10–20:9, 20–30:6. What is the total frequency?
Scores — 0–50:5, 50–100:12. How many scored at least 50?
Bins 0–20:6, 20–40:10, 40–60:4. Which interval is most common?

topics.name: Line Graphs
topics.details: A line graph shows how a quantity changes over time, with points joined by line segments. The steepness of each segment shows how fast the value is changing: a steep upward segment is a large increase, a downward segment a decrease, and a flat segment no change. Questions ask for the value at a given time, the change between two times (subtract the two values), the net change from start to end, or the interval with the greatest rise or fall (the steepest segment). Read values off the vertical axis carefully and watch the direction of change.

solved.problem: Temperatures: 6am 14°, 9am 18°, noon 25°. What is the rise from 6am to noon?
Using the same data, the change from 6am to 9am?
Values 10, 14, 13, 20 over four hours. Between which hours is the biggest rise?
solved.solution: The jumps are +4, −1, +7; the largest is the 3rd to 4th (+7).

solved.problem: A graph starts at 30 and ends at 22. What is the net change?

unsolved.problem: Sales: Jan 200, Feb 260. What is the increase?
Temps 12°, 17°, 15°. What is the change from first to second reading?
Values 5, 9, 8, 16. Which step is the largest rise?
A line goes from 50 down to 35. What is the net change?
Readings 20°, 20°, 27°. What is the change in the second interval?

topics.name: Scatterplots
topics.details: A scatterplot shows paired data as points, one axis per variable, revealing the relationship between them. If the points trend upward left-to-right the variables have a positive association; downward is a negative association; no pattern means no association. The closer the points lie to a straight line, the stronger the association. A line of best fit (trend line) summarises the pattern and lets you predict a y-value from an x-value by substituting into its equation. On the SAT, expect to identify the type of association, read or use a line of best fit, and make predictions — substitute carefully and follow the trend.

solved.problem: Points rise from left to right close to a line. What association is this?
solved.solution: An upward trend means a positive association.

solved.problem: A line of best fit is y = 5x + 10. Predict y when x = 4.
As a car’s age rises, its value falls. What association?
solved.solution: One up while the other down is a negative association.

solved.problem: Line of best fit y = 3x + 2. Find y at x = 6.

unsolved.problem: Points scatter with no clear direction. What association?
Line of best fit y = 2x + 7. Predict y at x = 5.
Hours studied vs score: points rise to the right. Association?
Line of best fit y = 4x + 1. Find y at x = 3.
Points lie very close to an upward line. Is the association weak or strong?
hints: Closeness to the line sets strength.
